item.title: Stream low-latency speech from AI agents using Kokoro TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
item.abstract: A customer asks an AI voice agent a question and waits. The agent already has an answer, it’s midway through generating a long, multi-paragraph response, but the customer hears nothing for five seconds. By the time an answer arrives, the customer is frustrated, confused, and no longer paying attention. Text-to-speech integrations create exactly that gap. A one-sentence response might generate in 600 milliseconds, but the full response takes five seconds, and the integration waits for all of it before synthesis starts. This post shows how to close that gap. We stream each sentence to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech (TTS) model on Amazon SageMaker AI as soon as an agent produces it, so synthesis begins on sentence one instead of the finished response. Getting that audio back to a browser needs its own solution too, so we also cover both transports for doing it and what each costs in practice. This solution closes the gap by streaming synthesis alongside generation instead of waiting for it to finish. As the agent produces each sentence, that sentence streams immediately to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model, so audio playback can start before the agent finishes speaking its full response. Kokoro-82M holds only 82 million parameters, small enough to run cheaply on a single mid-tier GPU instance. That keeps both latency and inference cost low for a voice agent handling real traffic. Kokoro-82M runs in a custom container on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, on an ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance. The container exposes two routes: POST /invocations , which streams a response for one complete input, and WS /invocations-bidirectional-stream , which keeps one connection open across many messages in both directions. The following diagram shows the request path from client to model: Figure 1: Request path from the client to the SageMaker AI real-time endpoint over a bidirectional stream The walkthrough first deploys the endpoint and agent, then works through the client-side changes that make incremental streaming work end to end. The Kokoro-82M endpoint and the agent runtime deploy through two CLI tools, each wrapping its own AWS CDK stacks: speech-infra deploy provisions the Kokoro-82M endpoint. This includes the foundation and model-cache stacks that create the underlying IAM roles and sync the model’s weights into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). The endpoint stack then builds the container image and creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. agent-infra deploy provisions the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosting the Strands agent, which calls the endpoint you just deployed, so deploy the endpoint first. The bidirectional transport SageMaker AI uses delivers every piece of a client’s message to your container as a binary WebSocket frame. A common way to write a Starlette WebSocket handler is calling receive_text() , which reads message["text"] and raises KeyError if that key isn’t present. Because every message this client sends arrives as binary, that handler fails on every request. The failure is commonly misdiagnosed. A generic exception handler that forwards str(e) to the client turns KeyError('text') into an error frame reading 'text' , which looks like a missing field, not a framing issue. The endpoint itself reports InService throughout, since it accepts connections and responds to every message, with an error each time. Accept either frame type explicitly instead of assuming one will show up: This decodes bytes as UTF-8 when no text field is present, rather than assuming one frame type. Test it by sending a binary frame, because this failure mode produces a well-formed error frame and a healthy endpoint status, not an obvious crash. After your container finishes synthesizing one message’s audio, the instinct is to close the session, the way an HTTP cycle ends. That’s wrong here. After sending a message’s audio and a synthesis_complete control frame, the container loop should go back to waiting on receive() for the next message on the same, still-open session. Close the connection only when the client sends an explicit {"type": "close"} message. The following diagram shows one session carrying two sentences in sequence, closing only at the end: Figure 2: One bidirectional session carrying two sentences in sequence, closing only at the end This way, you can send several sentences, one after another, on one persistent session, with no reconnection cost between them. Closing eagerly after one response would force a new connection per sentence, undoing most of the latency benefit. With the session behavior in place, the client-side fix for the latency problem is a class that normalizes text arriving in two shapes: a complete string known up front, or a live token stream. It produces the same output either way: complete sentences, ready to send as soon as each one is complete. Call feed() once per fragment of text as it arrives. It returns any newly completed sentences, holding back trailing text. Call flush() once, at the end of input, to release whatever partial text remains even without trailing punctuation. This keeps a stream that ends before a period arrives from dropping a final sentence. This isn’t concurrent synthesis. Every bidirectional handler is a strictly sequential loop: receive a message, synthesize its audio, send that audio, send synthesis_complete , then receive the next message. Sentence two’s audio isn’t generated while sentence one’s still transmits. What incremental sending buys is narrower: synthesis on sentence one begins the instant it exists, rather than waiting for the full response. For a multi-sentence response with real generation time between its first and last sentence, that’s the entire latency win. We verified this against a live endpoint sending a three-sentence input over one session. All three chunks arrived with audio matching the text sent for each: Streaming text into the model incrementally solves half the problem. The other half is getting the resulting audio out to whatever renders it, commonly a browser. Most agent and chat frontends already stream text over Server-Sent Events (SSE): one-directional, and supported natively by most browsers. SSE is a text protocol, not built to carry a raw binary payload. A team adding voice to an existing SSE pipeline naturally reaches for the pattern it already has: base64-encode the audio and wrap it in a JSON event. We measured the cost of that approach across 24 clips, confirmed with Amazon Transcribe that quality didn’t differ across encodings, and compared MP3 against AAC: Base64 inflates every payload by close to the expected 33%. The subtler cost is frame alignment. SSE events are delimited by a blank line, but the audio inside is delimited into MP3 frames. The two schemes don’t necessarily align with how the transport chunks the data. In one measured response, four logical MP3 frames arrived as six delivery chunks, two ending mid-frame. A consumer that treats each delivery chunk as one complete unit fails on ordinary, healthy traffic. The fix buffers incoming bytes and acts only once a delimiter is found: The alternative used today for the model-facing leg skips base64 and SSE framing entirely. It multiplexes raw binary audio and JSON control frames over the same bidirectional session already carrying incremental text input, and tells them apart with one rule. A chunk that fails to decode as a JSON object is audio, forwarded as received, with no encoding step anywhere in the path. One edge case matters: raw PCM audio can legitimately begin with byte 0x7b , the ASCII character { , the same character that opens a JSON object. This rule avoids misclassifying that audio because it requires the entire chunk to parse as valid JSON, not its first byte alone, something a PCM frame will essentially never do.

item.title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
item.abstract: Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.” The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis. In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison. “There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.” In publishing these results , Microsoft joins Go o gle and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors. The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top. Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5. Accuracy improvements delivered by DxO (no budget constraints) on CPC over models prompted with baseline prompt across different large language models. Image Credits: Microsoft AI Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO. With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost. DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided. Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added. Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare. “I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.” Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later. “We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said. He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.” “As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.” Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings. “This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said. He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’. Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time. “We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.” Microsoft’s study in Science coincides with a manifesto of sorts around what it will take to build medical superintelligence, defined as “the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.” Microsoft hopes to move beyond benchmarking individual tasks — like answering medical exam questions and generating diagnoses — into integrating with clinicians and healthcare systems for better outcomes. “This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants, and that’s why we’re committed to doing everything we can to accelerate its introduction to the world,” Suleyman said, adding that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to the other frontier labs. Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts. “We have to have the absolute number one state-of-the-art medical clinical decision support products over the next few years,” Suleyman said.

item.title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
item.abstract: Hey all, Kartik from Omnara ( https://omnara.com ) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API. You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines. Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada. Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out: Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents. Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there. The entire codebase is open source at  https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara , and it’s self hostable, even on a single machine with docker compose. You can also use the hosted version at  https://omnara.com . Let me know what you think!

item.title: AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?
item.abstract:
Page content Today we’re publishing patching-bugs and regression-hunt , two plugins that let engineers delegate patch development and regression checks to agents. Our patching-bugs plugin reproduces reported bugs, develops fixes, and tests them. The regression-hunt plugin checks whether any changes break previously working and supported behavior. Engineers can direct the work and review their results; maintainers can supply their own security assumptions and patching requirements, so the agents work within the project’s rules. We built patching-bugs and regression-hunt through Patch the Planet , our joint initiative with OpenAI, where we’ve co-authored hundreds of security patches for widely used open-source projects. Motivated by our major successes on projects like Scapy , our plugins draw on our analysis of merged patches and thousands of our engineers’ Codex sessions. The plugins provide maintainers with a structured workflow, evidence, independent checks, and best practices to improve their patching hygiene. In our preliminary evaluations, regression-hunt produces 25% fewer false-positive findings than a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.” Standardizing the patching process Our September post reported regressions introduced by some of our Patch the Planet patches. Since then, we’ve reviewed every patch that a Trail of Bits engineer authored and maintainers merged upstream. The review confirmed 21 regressions from over 130 PRs merged: 16 functional, one performance, and four build/test. None broke a security protection. (“Regression” refers to a new defect introduced by a change that breaks previously correct and supported behavior along a path a real user or attacker can reach.) For each patch, an agent looked for potential regressions, confirmed each one with a proof-of-concept (PoC) run before and after the change, and then passed the results to an engineer for review. The review was noisy: today’s bug disclosures arrive at an unprecedented speed and scale, and for patching to keep pace, the industry needs to increase its signal-to-noise ratio. The 21 confirmed regressions were identified among 58 candidates in a single run (~36% precision). But because agents take many different approaches and reach different results, each run generates more candidates to manually sort through. That led us to two conclusions: To introduce fewer regressions, we needed a standard way to write patches, with the same checks applied every time. To catch the regressions we still introduce, we needed a standard way to check for them, with written rules for what counts as a regression. Standardizing both steps also makes every run repeatable and comparable. No fixed checklist will catch every regression, so we collect agent trajectories from our engineers’ patching sessions, and use the tasks that an earlier version failed to benchmark for the next one (figure 1). Figure 1: Feedback loop for generating and evaluating patches. How we designed the plugins We used two primary sources to guide the design of our plugins: a review of every patch we merged upstream and the thousands of Codex sessions our engineers used to write those patches. This led to four principles that shaped our patching-bugs and regression-hunt plugins: Opinionated guidance in as few words as possible. We give the agent wide latitude and record only Trail of Bits’ judgment of what constitutes a good patch and a real regression. The goal is to direct the agent towards the desired result with the least possible guidance. Modular steps. You don’t have to run either plugin end-to-end, as both provide multiple skills that can be used in tandem or in isolation. Strict input and output schemas. Every step takes and returns a defined schema that includes the claim, the code revision, the required check, the raw evidence, and open questions. Fixed schemas reduce variability across runs and allow each step to verify the previous step’s work rather than trusting its summary. A live proof of concept for every claim. Every conclusion depends on a PoC run against a live deployment: a built, running instance of the project, reached through the interfaces a real user would use. When reproducing a bug, proving a fix, and confirming a regression, if a step can’t produce a live PoC, its result is inconclusive. regression-hunt reduces false positive rates The regression-hunt plugin (Figure 2): Enumerates candidate regressions by tracing the changed code (the diff) through its callers to its real interfaces. Reproduces each candidate regression on a live deployment of the system. Replays the PoC on the live deployment on a fresh-context agent. Judges the results of all the previous steps to validate that the proof meets the requirements of a regression. Figure 2: The regression-hunt workflow. In addition to the four principles above, there are two core aspects that are critical to the plugin: Defining a regression: The plugin has strong opinions about what a regression is and, more importantly, what a regression is NOT. The burden of proof is placed on the agent (specifically during the “adjudication agent” step) to prove that there is sufficient evidence to show that the suspected regression is not a false positive, an incomplete fix, a latent bug, a pre-existing bug, and so on. The plugin only reports a regression if all of these gates are passed. Incorporating a threat model: If a threat model is available, the orchestrator will intentionally pass this document as part of the global context for each individual agentic step. This is an attempt to require each step/agent to refer back to the threat model before reaching its conclusion. Our review of merged PRs yielded a set of 21 confirmed regressions that we could use to evaluate regression-hunt. We used the whole set to compare the plugin with a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.” Across those runs, regression-hunt produced 25% fewer false-positive findings than the baseline, with a 95% confidence interval of 14% to 38%. Its strict evidence requirements also left some known regressions classified as borderline: the plugin identified a possible regression but did not gather enough evidence to confirm it. Fewer false positives therefore came with a tradeoff in how many known regressions it could confidently report. Next, we’ll investigate why these cases remained borderline and improve the plugin’s strategies for gathering evidence. Our goal is to confirm more real regressions while giving maintainers clearer information when the evidence remains inconclusive. patching-bugs streamlines best practices from thousands of agent sessions The patching-bugs plugin is a distillation of all the best practices we’ve identified by analyzing thousands of Codex sessions by Trail of Bits engineers (Figure 3). In addition to the more traditional capabilities (such as reproduction on live deployments and independent adversarial review), the plugin emphasizes: The three-arm proof : The proof runs the same reproduction against three specifications: the original code must fail, the patched code must pass, and a complete revert must fail again. Bringing the bug back by removing the patch provides stronger evidence that the patch—rather than an unrelated environment or test change—actually fixed the bug. Invariant-guided repair: The patch attempts to fix the underlying, violated security invariant rather than fix the specific bug. This helps generalize the patch for possible variants of the same bug class. Incorporates regression analysis: The plugin mandates that regression-hunt is run to ensure that any patch goes through the same standard pipeline to check for mistakes. Figure 3: The patching-bugs workflow. What’s next for the plugins Both patching-bugs and regression-hunt will continue to evolve.

item.title: LeCun押注的世界模型，中國一家清華系公司已經做進了機器人
item.abstract: LeCun押注的世界模型，中國一家清華系公司已經做進了機器人 田, 晏林 2026-10-21 15:15:05 來源： 量子位 世界模型賽道新看點：千訣隱變數可辨識性方向的研究，比LeCun相近工作早一年，不堆畫面預測，主打物理規律與跨本體複用。 田晏林 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 世界模型這條賽道，越來越有全球頂尖AI高手過招的架勢了！ Yann LeCun持續押注預測式世界模型，李飛飛帶領World Labs探索可互動的3D世界，全球頭部AI團隊正沿著不同技術路線加速探索。 讓AI真正理解物理世界、預測物理變化，正成為新一輪技術競爭的焦點。 最近，這股世界模型熱潮也延伸至南京。 10月20日， 首屆2026物理AI與世界模型大會 在南京開幕。圖靈獎得主 LeCun、姚期智 都遠端分享了最新觀察。 在這場世界模型領域的學術與產業盛會上，清華系具身智慧公司 千訣科技 ，也在大會上正式釋出了 預測式世界模型Polibrain 。 千訣科技創始人高海川 在開幕式演講中，用一句話解釋了世界模型的獨特價值： 有了地圖，可以推匯出最短路徑；但有了路徑，並不能反過來推匯出一張地圖。 這裡的「地圖」，正是對物理世界及其變化規律的一種抽象理解。 而千訣此次釋出的Polibrain，想做的就是讓機器人擁有這樣一張可以用於預測和規劃的「地圖」。 早在2025年，千訣聯合清華大學團隊就在ICML發表了世界模型相關理論研究，其在隱變數可辨識性、低階偏好等方向上的公開探索， 比LeCun團隊的相近研究早了約一年。 僅僅一年後，千訣已經把相關技術積累推進到了真實機器人應用中。 從環境感知、行動預測，到自主規劃和執行反饋，千訣試圖讓機器人學會根據物理世界的變化，自主決定下一步怎麼做。 目前，這套智慧能力 已在四足、人形、輪式、雙臂等機器人形態上開展適配。 千訣的預測式世界模型Polibrain，究竟有什麼特別之處？他們又是如何讓不同形態的機器人，共用一套智慧大腦的？ 機器人大腦有了新解法 “世界模型講了這麼多，大家真的理解了嗎？” 在開幕式的壓軸演講上，高海川率先丟擲了這樣一個問題。 隨後，他講了一個「古代商人從廣州運送荔枝到長安，怎樣才能找到最快的路線？」的故事。 看過電影《長安的荔枝》的觀眾，對這個難題應該不陌生。 高海川給出了兩種解法。 一種辦法，是把可能的路線都走一遍，從中找出最優解。 另一種方法，則是先弄清廣州到長安沿途有哪些城市、城市之間如何連線，畫出一張地圖，再根據地圖規劃路線。 前者被他用來類比當前的VLA路線，後者則對應世界模型的預測與規劃方法。 區別在於，機器人能否提前推演行動可能帶來的結果，減少實際試錯。 這正是千訣Polibrain預測式世界模型想要解決的問題。 那麼，這套方法放到真實機器人身上，能做什麼？ 千訣提供的一段應用演示影片，展示了一個直觀場景。 在戶外，一臺帶著機械臂、揹著回收筐的四足機器狗，正在執行垃圾回收任務。 它需要自主尋找地面上的垃圾，識別目標位置，移動過去，再規劃機械臂動作，將垃圾抓起來，放進隨身攜帶的回收筐。 看起來只是一套撿垃圾的動作，背後卻有一連串決策難題： 垃圾在哪裡？機器狗應該從哪個方向靠近？機械臂伸出去之後，能不能順利抓住目標？ 尤其是在真實環境中，物體的位置、空間關係都可能發生變化。機器人光知道下一步做什麼還不夠，還得提前判斷，這一步做下去會發生什麼。 這正是預測式世界模型想解決的問題。 Polibrain通過學習環境狀態、歷史資訊和行動結果之間的關係，在任務相關的潛在表徵空間中預測狀態變化。 這裡還有一個關鍵的技術選擇。 Polibrain並 不追求把未來的每一幀畫面完整生成出來 。 對於正在撿垃圾的機器人來說，地面是什麼顏色、背景有多少紋理，未必重要。 真正影響任務完成的是垃圾的位置、機械臂與目標的相對關係，以及抓取動作會如何改變目標狀態。 與其花費大量計算資源還原整個世界，不如集中預測那些真正影響行動的關鍵資訊。 高海川在演講中也強調： “世界模型要做好，關鍵在於狀態表徵。” 但預測得準只是第一步。 真實任務很難完全按照計劃推進。如果抓取失敗，或者目標位置發生變化，機器人還需要知道如何繼續。 Polibrain將環境感知、狀態理解、行動預測、任務決策、動作執行和反饋調整連線起來，形成持續決策閉環。 當執行結果與預測不一致時，模型可以根據新的環境狀態重新評估任務，調整後續行動。 它還支援通過關鍵特徵解碼，追蹤預期狀態與實際結果之間的偏差，為異常定位和任務恢復提供依據。 不過，這套機制在複雜場景中究竟有多可靠，還需要更完整的實測資料驗證。 而且，這張「地圖」，理論上並不只屬於某一種機器人。 人形機器人可以用機械手抓杯子，輪式單臂機器人也可以。 雖然本體結構和控制方式不同，但它們需要理解的物體關係、目標狀態及環境變化規律存在共性。 這意味著， 面向物理世界的部分智慧能力，有機會在不同機器人之間複用。 目前，千訣已在人形、輪式、單臂、雙臂等多種機器人形態上開展適配，探索陪伴服務、餐飲服務、物品整理及精細操作等任務。 不過，要讓不同形態的機器人真正共用一套智慧能力，光有環境預測還不夠。 模型必須從複雜的真實場景中，學到可以跨環境、跨任務複用的規律。 這就涉及千訣更底層的一項研究： 多項式表徵。 比LeCun相近研究早一年，千訣如何突破泛化難題？ 所謂「多項式表徵」，簡單來說，就是 通過一套數學方法， 讓AI從複雜環境中提取真正影響任務結果的關鍵變數， 減少對無關細節的依賴。 為什麼需要這項技術？ 機器人想要適應不同場景，繞不開一個難題： 泛化 。 比如，機器人在一個倉庫學會抓取，換到另一個倉庫，光照、背景、貨架位置一變，表現就可能大打折扣。 問題在於，模型訓練時，很可能記住大量與任務無關的細節。背景紋理、光照條件，甚至物體周圍的擺設，都可能被神經網路當成判斷依據。 這就容易造成 「特徵汙染」 。 另一種問題更隱蔽：模型可能誤認為經常同時發生的現象之間，存在因果關係。 高海川在演講中舉了一個例子。 主人出門前，從抽屜裡拿走鑰匙。這裡有三個事件：主人出門、主人拿走鑰匙、抽屜裡的鑰匙消失。 如果模型只學習事件之間的相關性，就可能錯誤地認為，只要主人出門，抽屜裡的鑰匙就會消失。 等到主人真的忘帶鑰匙，讓機器人幫忙尋找時，機器人反而可能判斷，主人既然已經出門，鑰匙肯定不在抽屜裡了。 顯然，這不符合真實世界的因果關係。 模型究竟是在死記硬背，還是學到了物理世界的規律？ 千訣希望通過多項式表徵，讓模型少記場景細節，多學可遷移的規律。 這條路線背後，有千訣持續數年的研究積累。 2025年，千訣聯合清華團隊在ICML發表《When Do Neural Networks Learn World Models?》，研究神經網路在什麼條件下，能夠從觀測資料中恢復隱藏的世界結構。 研究從 「多工學習」和「低階偏好」 入手，利用Fourier-Walsh變換分析 離散佈爾世界中的函式結構 ，解釋模型何時能夠辨識真實隱變數。 有意思的是，LeCun團隊也從相近的理論視角切入。 2026年5月，LeCun等人發表《When Does LeJEPA Learn a World Model?》，同樣研究世界模型的隱變數可辨識性，以及函式階次與低階偏好之間的關係。 高海川在演講中進一步解釋了兩項研究的差異。 千訣團隊從因果推斷和布林空間的角度提出學習判據，LeCun團隊則從時間維度切入。 雖然研究物件不同，數學工具不同，但兩項研究提出的 學習判據 具有一定 等價性 ，最終匯出的表徵，在資訊層面也具有一定等價性。 事實上，兩者都在嘗試回答同一個問題： AI究竟如何從複雜觀測中，學到能夠泛化的世界結構？ 從公開發表時間看，千訣聯合清華團隊在相近方法論方向上的研究，比LeCun團隊上述論文早了約一年。 2026年，千訣聯合清華團隊進一步提出「有效階」 （Effective Degree，ED），試圖給神經網路的複雜度提供一把可以計算的「標尺」。 以往Benchmark能告訴研究者模型答得對不對，研究者卻不容易判斷模型學到的函式究竟有多複雜。 ED嘗試解決這個問題。 其方法是沿真實資料點之間的插值路徑觀察神經網路，用正交多項式擬合模型輸出，再根據不同階次成分的權重計算複雜度。 低階成分佔主導時，ED較小；高階成分越多、幅度越大，ED就越高。 這樣一來，研究者不僅可以量化、比較模型的函式複雜度，還能將這一指標引入訓練過程，幫助模型減少不必要的複雜變化。 當然，函式更簡單，不意味模型一定掌握了正確的物理規律。 但這項研究 為分析和最佳化模型泛化能力提供了新工具 。 除了學會提取規律，機器人還得記住真正重要的事。 比如，機器人把杯子放進櫃子，關門後就看不見了。等到下一步需要操作這個杯子，必須記得杯子被放在哪裡。 在連續任務中，物體可能被遮擋，部分狀態無法僅憑當前畫面判斷。 於是，千訣團隊還研究了 基於反事實推斷的歷史資訊篩選機制 。 簡單來說，就是判斷某段歷史觀測是否會影響後續預測和決策，再決定是否保留。 機器人無需記住看到的所有畫面，而是重點保留那些會影響後續任務的資訊。 背景是什麼顏色，不一定重要；杯子放進哪個櫃子，卻會影響下一步動作。 「多項式表徵」幫助模型提取關鍵變數，「因果記憶」則幫助模型篩選重要經歷。 兩者共同為機器人應對遮擋、延遲反饋、多步驟任務等複雜情況提供方法支援。 不過，相關基礎研究提供的是技術依據，實際效果還需要更多真實任務驗證。 總不能機器人每換一個房間，就重新學習一遍怎麼幹活吧？ 多項式表徵與因果記憶，為模型學習和利用可遷移的規律提供了技術基礎。 但學到的規律，怎麼才能讓不同形態的機器人共同使用？ 這就涉及另一個問題：如何把對世界的理解，與具體執行動作的機器人本體分開。 不造機器人，千訣想做所有機器人的大腦 說回那顆要送往長安的荔枝。 即便已經有了地圖，想把荔枝真正送到長安，也還需要馬匹、車船、驛站等不同運輸環節協同工作。 同樣，機器人有了對世界的理解，也不意味著它必須獨立完成所有動作。 高海川舉例說，讓機器人把衣服放進洗衣機，人形機器人可以一隻手拿衣服，另一隻手開門。 但如果換成只有一隻機械臂的輪式機器人呢？ 它完全可以通過智慧家居IoT系統，讓洗衣機自己開啟門。 硬體不同，執行方式不同，但最終對物理世界產生的變化可以相同。 這也是 千訣「松耦合世界模型架構」 想要解決的問題。 具體來說，Polibrain將面向環境與任務的共用表徵，與具體機器人的動作執行能力相對分離。 對世界的理解可以共享，至於怎麼執行，則由不同機器人甚至自動化裝置根據自身能力決定。 這套思路也決定了 千訣的產品定位：不造機器人本體，而是為不同形態的機器人提供智慧能力。 而且，千訣的目標不只包括 通用機器人 ，也包括 面向具體任務的專用機器人 。 高海川認為，具身智慧的商業落地可能是漸進的，不必一開始就追求完整的人形形態。 比如，減少一隻機械臂，可以成為酒店配送機器人；換成雙臂，可以進入餐飲服務場景；進一步調整本體結構，又能用於巡檢、安保、環衛清潔等任務。 形態可以因場景而變，底層對世界的理解卻有機會複用。 更值得關注的是，這種跨本體複用還有一層 資料價值 。 具身智慧長期面臨物理互動資料不足的問題。真機採集成本高、積累緩慢，不同形態的資料又難以直接共享。 從資料來源看，可以將機器人學習所需的資料大致分為三個層次： 底層是第一視角影片、人類操作影片等無本體資料，幫助模型學習環境、物體關係及互動過程。 中層是真機遙操等機器人本體資料，建立具體動作與物理環境變化之間的聯絡。 頂層是真實業務場景中的反饋資料，讓模型發現長尾問題，並持續迭代。 三類資料各有作用，但要讓它們真正產生價值，還需要解決跨本體資料難以複用的問題。 高海川認為，人形、輪式、四足乃至掃地機器人，雖然結構不同，但對物體關係、任務目標和環境變化的理解存在共性。 Polibrain希望通過共享高層表徵，讓不同形態積累的資料有機會服務同一套模型。 更多機器人接入，覆蓋更多真實場景；資料持續積累，推動模型泛化；模型能力提升，又有機會吸引更多機器人廠商和客戶。 由此，一套跨本體資料飛輪有了形成的可能。 不過， 共用表徵不代表資料就能自動打通。 高海川也提到了不同機器人企業之間的資料壁壘。 對於各家本體廠商而言，資料本身具有商業價值，開放共享並不容易。 千訣作為獨立模型公司，正在通過服務不同機器人企業，探索跨本體資料的協同利用。 從理論研究到真實機器人的應用，Polibrain的釋出，為預測式世界模型走向產業應用提供了一個觀察樣本。 item.title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
item.abstract:
Back to Articles Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 13 +7 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less
guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from
Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ],
) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" ,
) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 ,
) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast
combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations
have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" ,
) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models
forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit
the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results
with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores
are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations.
Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations.
